headline: High-risk shared filesystem and write-capable pair create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystem content, and agent_a also uses MCP while agent_b can run browsers and process files. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge through shared files or generated artifacts, even though no direct shared channel is documented. The pair is not provably isolated.
conditions: IF agent_a writes attacker-controlled text into a shared repo file that agent_b later parses as instructions
IF agent_b ingests file content from the shared workspace without provenance checks
mitigations: Restrict both agents to separate working directories
Disable MCP for agent_a unless provenance filtering is enabled
Require manual review of any file that crosses from agent_a to agent_b
Use allowlisted file types for inter-agent handoff
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a touches source code, git history, shell environment, and secrets in the invoking user context; agent_b touches text, images, audio, video, and multimodal data. Because both can read/write the filesystem and agent_a shares state via filesystem and git, sensitive material can flow from one agent to the other in default workspace setups.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same workspace or repo checkout
IF agent_a writes secrets or git history into files that agent_b can read
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Remove secrets from shared directories before handoff
Mount sensitive directories read-only for agent_b
Rotate any exposed credentials after a shared run
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and shell execution, and agent_a explicitly modifies git state while sharing state via filesystem and git. In a shared checkout, concurrent edits can overwrite each other or corrupt repository state without locking. The overlap is direct and dangerous in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same git repository
IF either agent writes while the other is rebasing, committing, or editing the same files
mitigations: Assign separate branches per agent
Pause one agent before the other writes to the repo
Use git worktrees for isolation
Run a quick diff before any commit
requires-engineering: add file locks or an orchestrator mutex

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_a can generate code or shell changes that agent_b may consume as input, and agent_b has enough execution capability to act on those outputs. No verification or provenance mechanism is documented between them, so an error in agent_a can propagate into agent_b's downstream actions.
conditions: IF agent_b treats agent_a's output as authoritative without independent checks
IF agent_a emits malformed commands, code, or facts that agent_b executes or renders
mitigations: Require a human review step between agents
Add schema validation for handoff artifacts
Have agent_b re-run critical checks independently
Limit agent_a output to structured data only
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware verification

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_a explicitly handles git credentials and shell environment data, while agent_b processes broad multimodal content and can read files. If regulated or personal data is placed in the shared workspace, the pair can create retention and residency mismatches through shared files and external API calls. No documented compliance boundary is provided for either agent.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace
IF either agent uploads that data to an external service or retains it beyond policy
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared directories
Disable network egress for the agent handling regulated data
Set explicit retention and deletion rules before use
Log all cross-agent transfers for audit
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
